title: What is event time vs processing time in Structured Streaming, why does the distinction matter for correctness (late/out-of-order events get bucketed by when they happened, not when Spark saw them), and how do you specify the event-time column?
shortTitle: Event time vs processing time in Structured Streaming

s1_definition.profdef: Event time is the timestamp recorded inside the event itself, marking when the thing actually happened at the source, whereas processing time is the wall-clock time on the Spark executor when the event is processed. The distinction matters because networks and systems introduce delays, so events arrive late and out of order; if you window by processing time you bucket events by when Spark happened to see them, which produces wrong aggregates, while windowing by event time buckets each event into the time window in which it truly occurred, giving correct and reproducible results regardless of arrival order. You specify the event-time column by making it a timestamp column in the streaming DataFrame and using it in your window and watermark definitions, for example `groupBy(window(col("eventTime"), "1 minute"))` with `withWatermark("eventTime", "10 minutes")`.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India a transaction slip is stamped with the exact moment it happened at the branch — that stamp is event time. The moment the central office opens the envelope and records the slip is processing time. If a slip is delayed in the post and arrives an hour late, you must file it under the hour it actually happened (event time), not the hour you opened the envelope (processing time); otherwise your hourly totals are wrong. Structured Streaming lets you file every transaction by its real stamp, so even a late-arriving slip lands in the correct hour's total.
s1_definition.oneliner: Event time is when it happened at the source, processing time is when Spark saw it — bucket by event time so late and out-of-order events still land in the correct window.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Event time is the timestamp recorded inside the event itself, marking when the thing actually happened at the source, whereas processing time is the wall-clock time on the Spark executor when the event is processed. The distinction matters because networks and systems introduce delays, so events arrive late and out of order; if you window by processing time you bucket events by when Spark happened to see them, which produces wrong aggregates, while windowing by event time buckets each event into the time window in which it truly occurred, giving correct and reproducible results regardless of arrival order. You specify the event-time column by making it a timestamp column in the streaming DataFrame and using it in your window and watermark definitions, for example `groupBy(window(col("eventTime"), "1 minute"))` with `withWatermark("eventTime", "10 minutes")`.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India a transaction slip is stamped with the exact moment it happened at the branch — that stamp is event time. The moment the central office opens the envelope and records the slip is processing time. If a slip is delayed in the post and arrives an hour late, you must file it under the hour it actually happened (event time), not the hour you opened the envelope (processing time); otherwise your hourly totals are wrong. Structured Streaming lets you file every transaction by its real stamp, so even a late-arriving slip lands in the correct hour's total.

**One line to remember:** Event time is when it happened at the source, processing time is when Spark saw it — bucket by event time so late and out-of-order events still land in the correct window.

sections.s2_technical:
Processing time is trivially available: it is just the clock on the machine when the record is handled. Early streaming systems windowed by processing time because it is easy, but it is wrong whenever events can be delayed. Two identical runs can produce different results depending on network timing, and a late event gets counted in the wrong window, so processing-time windows are neither correct nor reproducible for time-based analytics.

Event time is the timestamp embedded in the data — the moment the transaction was created at the branch, carried as a field in the Kafka message. Windowing by event time means an event that happened at 10:59 but arrived at 11:05 is still counted in the 10:00–11:00 window, because Spark uses the embedded timestamp, not the arrival clock. This makes aggregates correct and reproducible: replaying the same data always yields the same windowed result regardless of ingestion speed.

You specify the event-time column by ensuring it is a proper timestamp column in the streaming DataFrame, parsing it from the source if necessary, and then referencing it in the `window` function and the `withWatermark` call. For example `stream.withWatermark("eventTime", "10 minutes").groupBy(window(col("eventTime"), "1 minute"), col("accountId")).count()`. Spark now groups by the one-minute event-time window and keeps state for each open window.

The watermark is the mechanism that makes event-time windowing bounded. Because events can be arbitrarily late, Spark could keep every window's state forever. The watermark declares how late an event may be — for instance ten minutes — so Spark tracks the maximum event time seen, subtracts the watermark delay to get the watermark boundary, drops events older than that as too late, and finalizes and clears the state for windows that close before the watermark. Without a watermark, event-time aggregation state grows without bound.

A senior-level nuance is the trade-off encoded in the watermark delay. A larger delay tolerates later events and improves completeness but holds state longer and delays finalization, while a smaller delay finalizes faster and uses less memory but drops more late events. In banking you tune this to the real lateness distribution of the feed, often sizing the watermark to cover the 99th-percentile delay so you capture almost all events without unbounded state. Choosing event time plus an appropriate watermark is therefore a correctness-versus-resource decision, not a mere API detail.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India computes per-minute transaction counts. A branch transaction that happened at 10:59:30 arrives at the stream at 11:00:20 because of a network delay. If bucketed by processing time it would wrongly land in the 11:00 minute; bucketed by event time it correctly lands in the 10:59 minute.

Problem 2 — Some events arrive very late, hours after they happened. Without a bound, Spark would keep every minute's state forever. A ten-minute watermark drops events later than that and clears state for closed windows.

Problem 3 — The analytics team needs reproducible hourly reports: rerunning yesterday's data must give the same numbers. Event-time windowing guarantees this because the result depends on embedded timestamps, not ingestion timing.

The demo assigns each simulated transaction both an event-time minute and a (later) processing-time minute, then buckets the same events by each clock to show that only event-time bucketing places a delayed transaction in the correct minute, and it drops events beyond the watermark.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four transactions. SAV2001 at event minute 59 but processing minute 60 (delayed). CUR3001 at minute 60. A second SAV2001 at minute 60. An OLD0001 at event minute 40, far behind.

Step 1: Event-time bucketing runs. The maximum event minute is 60, and with a watermark delay of 10 the boundary is minute 50. OLD0001 at minute 40 is below 50, so it is dropped as too late.

Step 2: The remaining three are bucketed by their event minute. One transaction lands in minute 59 (the delayed SAV2001), and two land in minute 60. The correct per-minute counts are minute 59 has one and minute 60 has two.

Step 3: Processing-time bucketing runs. Every transaction used minute 60 as its arrival time, so all four (including the dropped-by-watermark OLD0001, which processing time does not drop) land in minute 60, giving a wrong count of four in minute 60 and nothing in minute 59.

Step 4: The demo logs both results so the engineer sees that only event-time bucketing places the delayed transaction in minute 59 and bounds state via the watermark.

Final output:

```
2026-10-30 05:06:30 INFO    Event-time minute counts (correct):     {59=1, 60=2}
2026-10-30 05:06:30 INFO    Processing-time minute counts (wrong):  {60=4}
2026-10-30 05:06:30 INFO    Event-time vs processing-time comparison complete.
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Event time is the timestamp inside the event marking when it actually happened at the source, and processing time is the wall-clock time on the executor when Spark handles it. The distinction matters because real systems delay events, so they arrive late and out of order. If you window by processing time, you bucket events by when Spark happened to see them, which misfiles delayed events and makes two runs of the same data produce different answers. If you window by event time, each event lands in the time window in which it truly occurred, so a transaction that happened at 10:59 but arrived at 11:05 is still counted in the 10:59 window, and results are correct and reproducible.

You specify the event-time column by making it a proper timestamp field in the streaming DataFrame and referencing it in the window and watermark. In practice that is withWatermark on the event-time column followed by a groupBy on a window over that same column. The watermark is what makes event-time windowing bounded: it declares how late an event may be, so Spark tracks the maximum event time, drops events older than that boundary as too late, and finalizes and clears state for windows that close before the watermark. Without a watermark, event-time state grows forever.

At the National Bank of India I used event-time windowing for per-minute transaction counts. Branch apps stamped each transaction with the real event time, and the streaming job bucketed by a one-minute event-time window with a ten-minute watermark, so a transaction delayed in the network still landed in the correct minute and very late stragglers were dropped while state stayed bounded. I tuned the watermark delay to cover roughly the ninety-ninth percentile of observed lateness, trading a little extra state for near-complete capture. In interviews I summarize it as: bucket by event time for correctness and reproducibility, use processing time only when timing genuinely does not matter, and always pair event-time aggregation with a watermark to bound state and drop events that are simply too late.

keyPoints: Structured Streaming: micro-batch or continuous processing
Watermark: handle late data — discard after threshold
Checkpoint: fault tolerance — recover state on failure
